summary.summary: Stockton-on-Tees's 2024/25 treasury outturn shows total borrowing up £42.39m in the year to £150.78m at 31 March 2025, with the rise almost entirely short-term: £61.38m is now borrowed from other local authorities at 5.10% on effectively zero weighted-average maturity, after the council repaid £21m of LOBO loans (called by the lenders) and refinanced them in the local-to-local market where rates peaked near 6% in February-March 2025. As a result 43% of all debt matures within 12 months against a 25% self-imposed upper limit -- the only prudential indicator breached in the year. The council remains substantially under-borrowed (£35.94m below its £195.86m General Fund CFR), holds £39.35m of investments (mostly money market funds plus a £13.28m pooled property fund), and carries a £6.7m accumulated DSG schools deficit whose cash-flow borrowing cost (up to £300k) falls on the General Fund. It still holds £18.322m of pre-2021 commercial property investments it may seek to exit; financing costs were a low 2.3% of net revenue.

signals.headline: Maturity-structure indicator breached: 43% of borrowing matures within 12 months at 31 March 2025 against a 25% upper limit
signals.why: The council is outside its own refinancing-risk control, exposing it to rollover at short-term rates that spiked near 6%.

signals.headline: £64.71m (43%) of borrowing is under 12 months at 31 March 2025, including £61.38m from other local authorities at 5.10% on ~0-year weighted-average maturity
signals.why: A large, near-continuously-rolling short-term book leaves the council re-pricing debt whenever inter-authority rates rise.

signals.headline: Total borrowing rose £42.39m (39%) in the year to £150.78m at 31 March 2025, driven by short-term LA loans raised to repay £21m of LOBOs and cover cash flow
signals.why: A sharp one-year jump in gross debt, concentrated in the most rate-sensitive, shortest-dated instruments.

signals.headline: Accumulated DSG (schools) deficit of £6.7m at 31 March 2025, cash-flowed through borrowing at a cost of up to £300k charged to the General Fund
signals.why: The schools deficit sits behind the statutory override but still creates a real cash and borrowing-cost drag on the General Fund.

news_drafts.headline: Stockton's schools funding deficit costs up to £500k a year in interest
news_drafts.lead: Stockton-on-Tees has accumulated a £17.1m deficit in its schools funding, the government grant that pays for education, primarily because of costs for children with special educational needs and disabilities. Although a temporary government measure called statutory override keeps the deficit off the council's main balance sheet, cash must still be borrowed to cover the shortfall. The borrowing cost in 2025-26 was up to £500k, paid from the council's general day-to-day spending budget. Placement costs for children in care have also risen to require significant change, and an Ombudsman investigation has identified procedural failures in services for children with disabilities. The council has initiated reviews to address both issues.

news_drafts.headline: Stockton-on-Tees council faces £5.8m revenue overspend with reserves at risk
news_drafts.lead:
The council is forecasting a £5.8m overspend on day-to-day spending of £293.8m, which it describes as a "significant financial challenge". If it materialises, reserves would fall to £16.3m by year-end, which the council states is "materially below the reserve levels assumed when the budget was approved in February and is not considered sustainable over the medium term."

The pressures include a £15.2m overspend in the schools budget, particularly in the dedicated schools grant high needs block, the funding for children with special educational needs. Independent special school placements are £5.15m over and out-of-area placements £3.6m over. Children's external residential placements are £2.96m overspent. The new waste service, launched in April, is £1.1m over budget on vehicles.

The council expects the government to write off approximately £15.4m of a cumulative £17.13m schools funding deficit, with approval expected in October, but would still need to fund approximately £1.52m annually. For the coming year, the council must find £1.48m in savings, with larger gaps of £10.3m and £14.8m forecast in the following two years.

findings.paper_title: Sep 2026 - Risk and Activity Report Appendix
findings.headline: Bridge inspections are delayed; progress review scheduled for six months
findings.detail: Two Red controls relate to delays in completing full bridge inspections. Progress is scheduled to be reviewed again in six months (by March 2027). No detail is provided on inspection scope, reasons for delays, or expected remedial costs.
findings.matters: Delayed asset inspections suggest deferred maintenance and may indicate unplanned future capital expenditure requirements or latent safety issues
findings.quote: some delays in completing full bridge inspections, progress is due to be reviewed again in the next 6 months

findings.headline: Council is deliberately under-borrowed by £24.16m, using reserves to minimize interest costs, but will require substantial future borrowing.
findings.detail: The council's borrowing of £168.97m is £24.16m below its Capital Financing Requirement of £202.27m. This reflects a deliberate 'internal borrowing' strategy using reserves and working capital rather than external borrowing. While this reduces immediate interest costs, it depletes cash reserves and means the council will eventually need substantial new borrowing to meet its CFR.
findings.matters: The under-borrowed position means the council will need to move to substantial new borrowing in coming years as reserves deplete, affecting both timing and cost of refinancing.
findings.figures: Borrowing £168.97m; Capital Financing Requirement £202.27m; under-borrowed position £24.16m
findings.quote: The Authority pursued its strategy of keeping borrowing and investments below their underlying levels, sometimes known as internal borrowing, in order to reduce risk and keep interest costs low. At the year end the Council had an under borrowed position of £24m.

findings.headline: Commercial property investments of £14.89m flagged for future exit due to Prudential Code restrictions.
findings.detail: The council holds £14.89m in directly-owned commercial property, down from £18.32m in the prior year. These generate £0.917m annual income (6.16% return) supporting services. Due to changes in the CIPFA Prudential Code restricting PWLB borrowing for commercial yield investments, the council notes it 'will need to review the options for exiting these investments if there is an economical case to do so.'
findings.matters: The council's planned exit will affect both liquidity (property sale proceeds) and ongoing revenue (loss of £0.9m annual income), factors lenders consider when assessing financial resilience.
findings.figures: Commercial property holdings £14.890m (down from £18.322m prior year); investment income £0.917m (6.16% return)
findings.quote: The Authority currently holds £14.890m in commercial investments (2024-25 £18.322m) that were purchased prior to the change in the CIPFA Prudential Code. The Authority, as part of the updated code, in the future will need to review the options for exiting these investments if there is an economical case to do so.

findings.headline: £16m of LOBO loans face increased probability of call exercises as interest rates have risen.
findings.detail: The council holds £16m of LOBO loans with average rate 4.87% and weighted average maturity of 11.4 years. These give the lender an option to propose rate increases at set dates. The council notes that 'there is an increased probability of call options on the LOBOs being exercised by lenders' given elevated interest rates. If exercised, the council would have the option to accept the new rate or repay at par.
findings.matters: LOBO call exercises force refinancing events requiring cash and creating potential refinancing at unfavorable rates; lenders view this as material to debt risk profile.
findings.figures: £16.0m LOBO loans; average rate 4.87%; weighted average maturity 11.4 years
findings.quote: On 1st April 2025 the Authority held £16m of LOBO (Lender's Option Borrower's Option) loans... As market interest rates have risen, there is an increased probability of call options on the LOBOs being exercised by lenders.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure came in at 54% of budget, £43.35m under the £94.53m estimate, with no explanation provided.
findings.detail: Capital spending was £51.2m against a budget of £94.53m, a shortfall of £43.35m (46%). Capital borrowing was correspondingly low at £6.93m against estimate of £23.1m. The council notes only that the variance was 'due to a variance against the in-year spend profile within the capital programme' without explaining the reasons for this substantial underspend.
findings.matters: A 46% capital underspend raises questions about project delivery capability and planning, affecting lender confidence in the council's ability to execute its plans and finance director forecasts of future borrowing needs.

daily_post.headline: Council must still fund approximately £1.52m of 2026/27 DSG deficit even if reform plan approved
daily_post.lead: The council's ongoing financial sustainability depends on achieving the capital investment programme and generating projected cost reductions; a £1.52m annual gap represents ongoing structural pressure even with substantial government support
